questions.q: What is the minimum time period usually used to determine the climate of a place?
questions.a: The climate is typically determined over a period of 30 years or more. A student who answers "a few days" or "one year" confuses weather (daily changes) with climate (long-term average).

questions.q: If a city is located very close to the Equator, how would you describe its climate compared to a city near the North Pole?
questions.a: The city near the Equator will have a warmer climate because it receives more direct sunlight. A wrong answer suggests the student does not understand how latitude affects solar radiation intensity.

questions.q: Why does a place at a very high altitude, like a mountain peak, often have a cold climate even if it is located in a tropical region?
questions.a: As altitude increases, the air becomes thinner and cooler, causing lower temperatures at higher elevations. A wrong answer shows a failure to connect height above sea level with temperature drop.

questions.q: How does the distance from the sea influence the climate of a coastal city like Mumbai compared to a landlocked city like Delhi?
questions.a: Coastal cities like Mumbai have a more moderate climate due to the cooling and warming effects of the sea, whereas inland cities experience more extreme temperature differences. A wrong answer indicates confusion about the temperature-regulating role of large water bodies.

questions.q: Is it accurate to say that if it rains heavily today in a desert, the climate of that desert has changed? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, it is not accurate, because climate is an average over many years; one day of rain is just a weather event. A wrong answer reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of the stability of climate versus the variability of weather.

questions.q: If you were asked to design a house for a place with a tropical, humid climate, what features would you include to keep it comfortable?
questions.a: The house should have high ceilings, large windows for ventilation, and materials that don't trap heat. A poor answer fails to connect the "warm and humid" description of the climate to practical living solutions.
